question: Can a recurrent network coupled to a differentiable external memory, read and written by attention, learn simple algorithms (copy, sort, recall) from input-output examples and generalise beyond the training lengths?
hypothesis: Coupling a controller to an addressable memory simplifies algorithmic tasks and yields solutions that generalise beyond the training range better than an LSTM alone.
contributions: A memory architecture (controller plus memory matrix with differentiable read and write heads) trainable end to end by gradient descent
A combined content-based and location-based addressing mechanism (interpolation, circular shift, sharpening)
A battery of five algorithmic tasks and a comparison of NTM (feedforward and LSTM controllers) against LSTM, with inspection of the learned memory-access algorithms

method.summary: An NTM pairs a controller network (feedforward or LSTM) with an N x M memory matrix accessed by read and write heads using soft attention weightings (content-based key matching by cosine similarity, then interpolation, circular-convolution shift and sharpening). Writes are erase then add. Trained with RMSProp on five synthetic algorithmic tasks and compared with a 3-layer stacked LSTM.
method.task: algorithmic sequence tasks: copy, repeat copy, associative recall, dynamic N-grams, priority sort

datasets.name: Copy
datasets.split: train on sequences of length 1 to 20 of eight-bit random binary vectors; tested up to length 120

datasets.name: Repeat Copy
datasets.split: train: sequence length and repeat count each random from 1 to 10, eight-bit vectors; repeat number input normalised to mean zero, variance one
datasets.preprocessing: repeat count normalised to mean 0, variance 1

datasets.name: Associative Recall
datasets.split: train: 2 to 6 items per episode; each item three six-bit binary vectors (18 bits); tested up to 20 items (Fig 11 axis)

datasets.name: Dynamic N-Grams
datasets.split: each training example: new random 6-gram table of 32 probabilities drawn from Beta(1/2,1/2), 200 successive bits drawn from it
datasets.source: synthetic; first 5 bits drawn i.i.d. Bernoulli p=0.5

datasets.name: Priority Sort
datasets.split: input 20 binary vectors with scalar priorities uniform in [-1, 1]; target the 16 highest-priority vectors sorted

models.name: NTM with feedforward controller
models.architecture: feedforward controller, memory 128 x 20, 1 to 8 heads depending on task
models.hidden: controller size 100 (copy, repeat copy, N-grams), 256 (associative), 512 (priority sort)
models.heads: 1 / 1 / 4 / 1 / 8 read-write heads (copy, repeat copy, associative, N-grams, priority sort)

other.shift_range: shifts -1 to 1 given as an example only; actual range not stated

models.name: LSTM
models.hidden: 3x256 copy, 3x512 repeat copy, 3x256 associative, 3x128 N-grams, 3x128 priority sort

other.learning_rate: 3e-5 copy, repeat copy, priority sort; 1e-4 associative, N-grams

training.objective: cross-entropy on binary targets with logistic sigmoid outputs; reported in bits per sequence
training.optimizer: RMSProp in the form of Graves 2013, momentum 0.9
training.lr: 1e-4 or 3e-5 depending on task and model (Tables 1-3)
training.regularisation: gradient components clipped elementwise to (-10, 10) in the backward pass

other.state_reset: dynamic state reset at start of each sequence: LSTM previous hidden state set to a learned bias vector; for NTM the controller state, previous read vectors and memory contents reset to bias values
other.training_length: learning curves run to about 1000 (thousand) sequences, 500 for repeat copy (read from Figs 3, 7, 10, 13, 18)

metrics.name: cost per sequence
metrics.definition: cross-entropy of the predicted binary sequence

baselines: optimal Bayesian estimator for dynamic N-grams
eval.protocol: learning curves per task; generalisation tested on longer sequences than seen in training; no repeated runs, seeds or significance tests reported (the text says 'small, but significant' for N-grams without a test)

evidence.where: Table 1 (feedforward controller row Associative has 4 heads, controller size 256)

results.claim: On copy, NTM with either controller learns much faster than LSTM and converges to lower cost.
results.setup: Copy task, eight-bit vectors, lengths 1-20, Fig 3
results.quote: learned much faster than LSTM alone, and converged to a lower cost

results.claim: NTM trained on copy lengths up to 20 continues to copy at longer lengths, while LSTM degrades rapidly beyond 20.
results.setup: Copy; test lengths 10, 20, 30, 50, 120 shown in Fig 4 and 5
results.quote: while LSTM rapidly degrades beyond length 20
results.note: Footnote: limiting factor was memory size of 128 locations, after which shifts wrapped and overwrote earlier writes. The length 120 example still has one global error (a duplicated vector).

results.claim: On associative recall NTM reaches near zero cost within about 30,000 episodes, while LSTM does not reach zero after a million.
results.setup: Associative recall, 2-6 items of 3 six-bit vectors
results.quote: terminating at near zero cost within approximately 30, 000 episodes, whereas LSTM does not reach zero cost after a million episodes

results.claim: On associative recall, the feedforward-controller NTM is nearly perfect up to 12 items (2x training max) and under 1 bit average cost at 15 items.
results.setup: Associative recall, trained on at most 6 items, feedforward controller NTM
results.quote: still has an average cost below 1 bit per sequence for sequences of 15 items

results.claim: Repeat copy: both NTM and LSTM solve the trained range, but only NTM generalises to longer sequences and more repeats; it cannot predict the end marker beyond training repeat counts.
results.setup: Repeat copy, length and repeats 1-10, doubled one at a time at test
results.quote: it is unable to keep count of of how many repeats it has
results.note: Fig 8 caption: end marker emitted after every repetition beyond the eleventh.

results.claim: On dynamic 6-grams NTM has a small advantage over LSTM but never reaches the optimal estimator.
results.setup: Validation set 1000 sequences of length 200, Fig 13 y-axis about 130-160 bits
results.quote: but never quite reaches the optimum cost
results.note: Text calls the advantage 'significant' without a stated test.

results.claim: Priority sort with a feedforward controller needed eight read and write heads for best performance.
results.setup: Priority sort, 20 inputs, top 16 as target
results.quote: eight parallel read and write heads were needed for best performance with a feedforward controller

results.claim: NTM parameter count does not grow with number of memory locations, while LSTM parameters grow quadratically with hidden units; LSTMs used here have far more parameters.
results.table: Table 1, row Copy, column #Parameters (17, 162); Table 3, row Copy, column #Parameters (1, 352, 969)
results.note: Numbers printed with a space after the comma in the extracted text.

limits: Authors call the experiments preliminary; only small synthetic algorithmic tasks, no real-world data.
No seeds, repeated runs, error bars, batch size, step counts or hardware stated.
Copy generalisation capped by memory size of 128 locations (footnote 2).
NTM cannot count repeats beyond the trained range; the authors attribute it to the numeric repeat encoding.
NTM does not reach the optimal estimator on dynamic N-grams.
Interpretations of learned algorithms (heap-sort hypothesis, pseudocode for copy) are inspection-based, 'we believe', not proved.
Not compared against any non-LSTM baseline; LSTM is much larger in parameters than NTM in most tasks.

terms.definition: the network outputs that parametrise the selective read and write operations on memory
focuses attention on locations based on the similarity between their current values and values emitted by the controller
addressing of a variable by its location (rotational shift of the weighting) rather than by content

lineage.note: LSTM is the baseline and one of the controllers; erase/add writes are inspired by its gates

lineage.work: Generating sequences with recurrent neural networks (Graves, 2013)
Neural machine translation by jointly learning to align and translate (Bahdanau et al., 2014)

lineage.note: gated working-memory model, no memory addressing
variable-binding critique of connectionism that the NTM answers
